issues.title: Spec is unclear on what a "syntactically valid email address" is
issues.author: cbiesinger
issues.body:
https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-00.html#section-4.2-6.2
> Verifying the email field contains a syntactically valid email address

It is not clear how this spec defines "syntactically valid email address".

comments.author: dickhardt

issues.title: Requested email is not part of the signature
issues.author: cbiesinger
issues.body:
https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-00.html#name-signature-input-header

> The covered components MUST include @method, @authority, @path, and signature-key. The cookie component MUST be included when the Cookie header is present, and MUST be omitted when it is not (per [[RFC9421](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-00.html#RFC9421)] Section 2.5). The created parameter MUST be included.

This does not include `Content-Digest` or any other way of including the email in the signature. This seems unintentional?

cc @yi-gu @samuelgoto

comments.author: samuelgoto
comments.body: I don't recall exactly why we didn't include `Content-Digest`, but seems reasonable to me to add to the signature. @dickhardt ?

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: @cbiesinger -- I was under the impression this would be challenging to do in the browser -- Content-Digest would need to be generated and set -- and then it could be included in Signature-Input -- will update in next version. New publications are effectively locked until after IETF.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Addressed in #16 (merged): the token request now carries a `Content-Digest` header (RFC 9530) over the request body, `content-digest` is a required covered component, and the issuer recomputes the digest against the received bytes before acting on the body. The requested email is now bound to the signature.

issues.title: §2.1 Email Discovery: where do suggested addresses come from?
issues.author: lonetis
issues.body:
§2.1 says:

> Before presenting the user with email address choices, the browser discovers which email accounts have active sessions with an issuer.

This reads as if the browser resolves an issuer *before* any email is known. But issuer discovery (§3) is a DNS lookup on the email's domain, so it can't run until an email is already selected. The two appear circular unless §2.1's discovery is understood as purely FedCM-based (issuer → emails via Push/Pull, no DNS involved).

The companion W3C Email Verification API describes the reverse ordering: the browser suggests addresses from its own autofill store, the user selects one, and only then are DNS issuer discovery and FedCM Accounts Validation run on the selection. There, FedCM is used to *validate* a pick, not to *source* the suggestions.

So the two documents seem to disagree on the origin of the suggested addresses: §2.1 has FedCM-discovered accounts populating the list pre-selection, while the W3C flow has browser autofill populating it and all issuer/FedCM involvement happening post-selection.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
@lonetis 
> §2.1 says:

> Before presenting the user with email address choices, the browser discovers which email accounts have active sessions with an issuer.

this sentence is confirming the email has an active session with an issuer for the domain -- which makes sense if we only support  there being a cookie -- but does not allow other options we are considering for the issuer to request the user to login when there is no cookie

DNS is always required for the browser and the verifier to know the issuer is truly authoritative for email verification independent of what FedCM accounts say

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Addressed in #20 and simplified further in #17 (both merged). Email Discovery now says: candidate addresses come from the W3C Email Verification API (browser store, FedCM push/pull, or typed) and are out of scope here; the browser offers only valid email addresses; and issuer discovery runs on the domain of whatever address the user selects — the DNS delegation alone determines the issuer, whatever the source.

issues.title: Nonce and Key Binding Issues
issues.author: dennisjackson
issues.body:
A comment I raised in the side-meeting: 

The current draft is a bit underspecified in terms of the privacy and security properties it's trying to achieve. For example, the decision to use a browser-based key to sign the RP's nonce means that sucessful logins to a RP may not be 1:1 with requests to the issuer. 

Concretely, an attacker who can perform the Issuance process once and receive a valid credential for a public key they control can then respond to arbitary challenges until the credential expires. If the client were using SSO style flow this would not be possible without the Issuer noticing (it seems strange that djackson has made 100 logins to different sites in the last minute). This would be prevented if the RP's nonce were also signed by the Issuer. If there are privacy concerns with exposing this to the Issuer (e.g. identifying the RP), a blind signature might be the right solution.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Before changing anything here I want to separate two things in this report, because I think one is a concrete defect and the other is a design question that deserves discussion rather than a patch.

**The concrete part.** The EVT has no `exp` claim. Verification says only "verify `iat` is within an acceptable time window" — in both the browser's and the RP's steps — and never says what that window is. So the credential lifetime your analysis turns on isn't just long, it's unspecified, and two RPs can disagree about whether the same token is live. That looks like a straightforward fix: add `exp`, have the issuer set it, and say what an RP does with it. I don't think anyone will object.

**The design question, which is the one I'd like discussion on.** "Successful logins to an RP may not be 1:1 with requests to the issuer" is true, and it is what the three-party model buys. The issuer not seeing 100 logins in a minute is the same property as the issuer not learning which RP the user visited. Making the issuer sign the RP's nonce would restore its visibility into presentation, and would cost exactly the privacy the design exists to provide. Your blind signature suggestion is the interesting thread precisely because it's the only version that might give both — but it's a substantial change and I'd want to know whether the resulting property is worth it before designing to it.

So, questions I'd like input on:

1. **How long should an EVT live?** If it's short enough — tens of seconds, roughly the span of one verification interaction — does the multi-presentation window close far enough to matter? The browser obtains the EVT and mints the KB-JWT immediately; there's no legitimate reason for a gap.

2. **Should an EVT be single-use?** Nothing currently says one EVT can't be presented to many RPs. A requirement that the holder use each EVT for exactly one RP would kill the "respond to arbitrary challenges" case directly, without the issuer learning anything. It's enforced by the browser rather than checked by the issuer, which is weaker — but the attacker in your scenario is running their own software anyway, so it's worth being explicit about what a rule on the holder actually buys against them.

3. **What is the residual threat if both are in place?** An attacker who completes issuance once, against their own account, holds a credential for an address they genuinely control. They can present it to several RPs within the lifetime. What's the concrete harm that isn't already available to someone who simply runs issuance per RP?

4. **Is blind signing worth prototyping?** If the answers above leave a real gap, this is where I'd go next, and I'd want to scope it as its own piece of work.

@dennisjackson — does splitting it this way match what you were getting at, or does the visibility point stand on its own independent of the lifetime question? Anyone else with a view on 1 and 2 in particular, that's the part I'd like to settle first.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: @dennisjackson -- would love to get more of your thoughts on this.

issues.title: Security Considerations around DNS Delegation
issues.author: dennisjackson
issues.body: Viktor pointed out that the DNS Delegation needs to be checked by the client, but clients struggle to validate DNSSEC or rely on DoH. Spoofed DNS records may lead to credential compromise with a user's mail provider (depending on how clients authenticate). Authentication decisions should only depend on information fetched via HTTPS and never from DNS (as a rule).

issues.title: Should `iss` should be a full origin?
issues.author: samuelgoto
issues.body:
In this example:

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-00.html#name-payload

```json
{
  "iss": "issuer.example",
  ...
}
```

The browser spec currently enforces that `iss` is a full origin (meaning, contains also a scheme, `https` specifically), so it expects something like the following:

```json
{
  "iss": "https://issuer.example",
  ...
}
```

I'm not sure which spec needs to change, but this is a difference between what has been implemented and what the spec says ...

... Should `iss` be an origin?

issues.title: Don't disclose private email address usage to websites
issues.author: ShivanKaul
issues.body:
As discussed in today's IETF side-meeting, `is_private_email: true` is currently required in the EVT as defined in [section 8.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-hardt-email-verification-01#name-requirements).

This is a privacy leak. Websites (relying parties) shouldn't need to know that a user is signing up with a private email address. This would give websites an easy way to block users who use email aliases.

comments.author: npdoty
comments.body:
It seems likely that directed identifiers / private email addresses may still be detectable by the relying party, e.g. by looking for long, high-entropy handles, or recognizing the separate domains that some email providers will use for that functionality. I expect (and the document should note in privacy considerations) that libraries/vendors will likely exist to try to distinguish private from non-private emails.

But I agree that it doesn't seem useful to provide a boolean in the response itself, when that seems to primarily enable coercion of the user.

issues.title: gmail email verifications don't have a kid
issues.author: LeviSchuck
issues.body:
Section 5.2 specifies: 

> Construct the header with alg, kid, and typ

What actually gets sent is `{"alg":"EdDSA","typ":"evt+jwt"}`, no kid claim inside

None of the keys have a kid claim: https://verifiablecredentials-pa.googleapis.com/.well-known/vc-public-jwks 

Section 5.3 specifies:

> Verify the EVT signature using the public key identified by kid

When there's no kid I have to verify against every key in the jwks until one works.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: @LeviSchuck known issue https://github.com/WICG/email-verification/issues/43

issues.title: private/directed identifiers seems to be optional afterthought, should be recommended or required
issues.author: npdoty
issues.body:
It seems like the only safe way that this system can be deployed is if issuers, at least primarily, provide directed identifiers rather than permanent cross-context addresses. Tracking users across contexts and selling their contact info for behavioral tracking and spam are lucrative for sites and only limited by the friction and cost involved in getting users to verify email addresses by delivering a message.

It appears that currently private or directed email addresses are optional, not included in the primary examples, and disabled by default. It seems that instead private email addresses SHOULD be used, with a fallback option for users or services that can't currently provide it and explicitly note that they don't offer that baseline protection.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: The directed identifiers are not an after thought, but are an exploration in feasibility and functionality.

issues.title: Why is `cookie` included in signature-input
issues.author: cbiesinger
issues.body:
https://dickhardt.github.io/email-verification/draft-hardt-email-verification.html#section-4.1.3

It is not clear to me what the value is of including this header. Also, this is difficult to implement (at least in Chrome) because the cookie header it not available at the point in time when the request is constructed.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: @cbiesinger  The cookie is what the issuer is using to authenticate the user. If impractical, we can make it optional.

comments.author: cbiesinger
comments.body:
> The cookie is what the issuer is using to authenticate the user

Yes but what is the value of including it in the signature...

I would appreciate it being optional, thanks!

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Addressed in #17 (merged): covering `cookie` is RECOMMENDED when the Cookie header is available to the signer at signing time, MUST be omitted when it is not, and an issuer MUST NOT reject a request solely because `cookie` is not covered. Examples no longer show it as a covered component, since the browser's network stack attaches the Cookie header after signing.

issues.title: Examples should included nonce
issues.author: cbiesinger
issues.body:
https://dickhardt.github.io/email-verification/draft-hardt-email-verification.html#name-token-request mentions the nonce but does not show it being used.

Per https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9421/#name-minimal-signature-using-rsa I believe the nonce should be included in the signature input (and therefore in the signature base).

comments.body:
https://dickhardt.github.io/email-verification/draft-hardt-email-verification.html#name-signature-input-header

It doesn't seem to me that `Signature-Input` includes `nonce` ... should it? 

Meaning, I don't think this is just simply an editorial issue in a comment, but rather a missing normative reference to `nonce` in `Signature-input`?

comments.body: It's not completely clear but https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9421/#name-minimal-signature-using-rsa sounded like nonce should be included as a parameter

issues.title: Should `email` always be the address exactly as provided?
issues.author: rowan-m
issues.body:
This occurred to me when seeing that Gmail was returning `email` in the token in the form `First.Last@gmail.com` when the user had entered `first.last@gmail.com`. (https://github.com/rowan-m/rowan-fyi/issues/58) . This only got picked up because the demo was mistakenly doing a case-sensitive comparison.

However, it occurred to me that users might provide an email address that is functionally equivalent if not exactly equal, e.g. `fir.s.t.last@provider.example` or `prefix+first.last@provider.example`.

I think that if the user supplies an email address that the provider validates, the provider should return the email address explicitly as supplied and not a canonical / normalised version of it. This also feels preferable from both a privacy point of view in that no additional information about the identity is shared back with the verifying site and simpler for the verifying site as well since they don't have to consider any provider-specific rules around transforming addresses.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Agreed the spec has to say something — right now it says nothing, which is how the Gmail `First.Last@` case got as far as a demo before anyone noticed. Before writing it I want to separate the case that's clearly a bug from the one that's a real design choice, because I don't think they have the same answer.

**Case 1: case folding.** `First.Last@gmail.com` for `first.last@gmail.com`. The domain is case-insensitive by RFC 5321, so an RP comparing domains case-sensitively is wrong regardless. The local part is formally case-*sensitive*, but essentially no provider treats it that way. I don't think there's much disagreement here: the spec should say how an RP compares two addresses, and probably say issuers shouldn't case-fold what the user supplied. That part I'd just fix.

**Case 2: canonicalization that changes identity.** Dots and `+` tags — `fir.s.t.last@` and `prefix+first.last@` resolving to the same mailbox. This is where I'd like discussion, because "return exactly as supplied" has a consequence worth being explicit about:

If the `email` claim is whatever string the user typed, then **the user chooses their own identifier at each RP.** One mailbox yields unboundedly many distinct `email` values. An RP doing account lookup by email address gets a different account per variant, so the same person signs up repeatedly at the same site without either party noticing. That's a real interop cost and it lands on RPs, who can't fix it without implementing provider-specific normalization — which is exactly what you're arguing they shouldn't have to do.

The counter-argument, which I find genuinely strong: returning the canonical form means the issuer tells the RP something the user didn't, and the `First.Last` capitalization is information about the account rather than about the address. Your privacy framing is right as far as it goes.

There's also a third option nobody has raised: if the concern is that the returned address leaks more than the user offered, private email addresses already solve that completely, and better than preserving the typed form does.

Questions:

1. **Should the `email` claim be a stable identifier for a mailbox, or a faithful echo of user input?** These conflict, and I'd rather the spec choose deliberately than leave it to each issuer.
2. **If it's the stable identifier**, is a MUST for the local part being returned as the issuer holds it acceptable, given RPs then get one value per mailbox?
3. **If it's the echo**, what do we tell RPs to do about the duplicate-account problem? "Compare case-insensitively" doesn't cover dots and tags.
4. **Does the answer differ for private addresses?** Those are issuer-generated, so there's no user-supplied form to preserve and the question may not arise.

My current lean is to fix the case-comparison issue now — that's unambiguous and it's the bug you actually hit — and settle the canonicalization question separately. @rowan-m does that split work for you, or do you see case and dots as the same question?

comments.author: rowan-m
comments.body:
Yeah, case-insensitive comparison seems like an easy inclusion. @samuelgoto also raised this in #24.

For the wider question, I'm leaning towards it being left as responsibility for the IdP to return an appropriately normalised version of the email address that the RP should consider canonical.

So, if someone is running their own catch-all domain with deliberate variations for spam tracking, then they can return what they want. A larger provider may choose to return a normalised version, e.g. `fir.s.t.last@example.com` > `first.last@example.com` if they deem it better for their users.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Addressed in #17 (merged): the address is never altered anywhere in the protocol. The browser offers only valid email addresses (the WHATWG production), sends the selected address byte-for-byte in the token request, and the issuer returns it byte-for-byte in the `email` claim. Every email comparison is byte-for-byte. The Gmail `First.Last@` case round-trips unchanged: what the user selected is what the RP receives.

issues.title: Consider allowing `email` to be an attribute from a selective disclosure rather than in the issuer's JWT
issues.author: samuelgoto
issues.body:
In [Token Verification](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-01.html#name-token-verification), specifically in [EVT Verification](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-01.html#evt-verification), `email` is required to be present in the "payload":

> Extract and validate the iss, iat, cnf, email, and email_verified claims from the payload

This disallows verifiers (of which there are many) to be forwards compatible with issuers that might want to issue the `email` attribute as a [SD-JWT](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-fett-oauth-selective-disclosure-jwt-02.html) selective disclosure (rather than a payload).

This is particularly problematic because it corners the protocol from ever having issuers that issue the `email` attribute as a selective disclosure, because that would require redeploying every verifier before issuers could make use of the feature.

It is unclear exactly what the use cases are for issuers to having the `email` attribute in selective disclosures (as opposed to the payload), but one of the open design alternatives that we explored was having a variation of the protocol that (a) doesn't contain `email` as an input to the [token request](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-01.html#name-token-request) and instead (b) asks the issuer to produce "all emails that the user is logged in to", allowing the browser/user agent to only selectively disclose the specific email that the user selected. This variation could be used as an alternative to the current imposition that the browser makes for the issuer to expose itself as a FedCM Login Status API provider and expose an [accounts endpoint](https://w3c-fedid.github.io/FedCM/#idp-api-accounts-endpoint) to list "all emails that the user is logged in to".

Because there are a really large number of verifiers, whatever gets ossified first is going to be really hard to change later, so, unless there are drawbacks to having verifiers ALSO accept the `email` attribute in selective disclosures, I'd recommend changing the [EVT verification](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-01.html#evt-verification) algorithm to allow them so that we can keep this door open if we ever need it.

Related discussion here: https://github.com/WICG/email-verification/issues/49

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Agree that getting verifiers to change to looking at an SD is much harder to do than including SD now. 

A major concern would be availability of SD libraries for verifiers -- would need some data to see support -- the current tokens are pretty easy to verify with widely available JWT libraries and a little string parsing on the `~` 

If we do support SD -- then I'd prefer that to be the ONLY way to send the email rather than two different ways.

comments.author: samuelgoto
comments.body: Supporting only in SD would be a backwards incompatible change but I think would be worth doing so that we can decouple the token from the email (eg if one wants to use this for handles rather than email).

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
@samuelgoto  I don't think the SD-JWT is as useful as you think it might be in the general case. 

The advantages of SD-JWT are:
- decoupling issuance and and presentation. There has been concern with that capability  #5  as the browser can now share present anywhere it wants, whenever it wants. 
- the browser can know which emails the issuer is authoritative for from the issuer. This may prove useful for issuers that manage mulitple emails for the same user -- but how common is that outside of Google and Hellō?

To know which issuer to call, the browser must somehow learn the issuer. Currently we are forcing the browser to go to the issuer to learn about the email addresses it supports -- but that is driven by privacy concerns. The verification protocol does not require that -- the browser can learn about an issuer by the user providing an email address. 

I don't see where there is much utility to this for the verification complexity it adds.

comments.author: samuelgoto
comments.body:
> This variation could be used as an alternative to the current imposition that the browser makes for the issuer to expose itself as a FedCM Login Status API provider and expose an [accounts endpoint](https://w3c-fedid.github.io/FedCM/#idp-api-accounts-endpoint) to list "all emails that the user is logged in to".

@dickhardt and I chatted over VC about this and he raised a good point: this can be accomplished by having the issuer return a list of JWT+KB tokens (rather than a single one) while still maintaining compatibility with verifiers.

I think that addresses my biggest requirement: finding a way to change how we issue EVTs without having to redeploy verifiers.

> I don't see where there is much utility to this for the verification complexity it adds.

I think this is raising another independent point, I'll kick off another issue to track this.

issues.title: Consider renaming headers to `username-*` rather than `email-*` to represent atproto and activitypub
issues.author: samuelgoto
issues.body:
I'm not entirely convinced this is necessarily a good idea, but I wanted to bring this up to make sure it doesn't fall through the cracks.

It has been noted, rightfully so, that the Email Verification Protocol has little to actually do with "email" per se, but can be actually (for better or for worse) only makes an assertion of "does the current user own this specific username X on domain Y" (rather than, for example, also make an assertion of email deliverability).

It is unclear if that's a feature or a bug, but this also just so happen to be the affordance that we need to prove ownership of ActivityPub handles (user@mastodon.com) and AtProto (@username.com).

Email Verification, I think, is a great scope to take and we should probably keep much of the API and interface email specific, but perhaps there is a way that we can have some basic infrastructure that is email-agnostic in case we want to anticipate how we would (or would not) extend this proposal to support activitypub and atproto handles.

A few possible outcomes comes to my mind:

1. keep the "Email Verification" scope but just change the headers / fields to use an email agnostic name, e.g. `.well-known/username-verification` rather than `.well-known/email-verification` (the `Sec-Fetch-Dest` and the `DNS TXT` record perhaps but maybe not the `email` attribute in the JWT?).
2. do nothing and maintain the `email-*` naming, and use those terms for activitypub and atproto
3. duplicate the protocol with `email-*` and `username-*` to support activitypub and atproto

It is not clear to me which option is best, but I just figured that if we do (2), we should do it deliberately rather than accidentally.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
I think it is better developer ergonomics to be consistent and use the same name everywhere. 

We call the mobile devices in our pockets a phone -- but 99% of the use is not making phone calls. 

The core use case is replacing email verification -- so more people will understand what it does with that name.

I do think that some signalling if there is deliverability could be useful.

comments.author: samuelgoto
comments.body:
I think this is a reasonable resolution. Closing.

> I do think that some signalling if there is deliverability could be useful.

I think this is a very different issue, so closing this one and kicking another one to capture this.

issues.title: Post Quantum algorithms?
issues.author: samuelgoto
issues.body:
This came up in passing and I figured it would be useful to file to make sure it doesn't fall through the cracks.

Do we have a PQ story? Can / have we picked algorithms that are PQ safe? If so, feel free to close this. If not, do we know how to go through a PQ transition?

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
PQ algs are  in https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose#web-signature-encryption-algorithms

We just list the ones supported in the metadata -- alg agility is designed in. Closing unless someone knows otherwise.

issues.title: Be explicit about case insensitive email matching
issues.author: samuelgoto
issues.body:
In section https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-hardt-email-verification-01.html#section-5.3-4.1, where it says:

> The email claim matches the email address being verified

We should go over explicitly the type of matching that we are making, which, specifically, ignores case sensitivity, so that verifiers don't reject emails that the browser otherwise accepts.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Addressed in #17 (merged), by removing the need for a matching rule rather than defining one: nothing in the protocol ever alters the address. The browser sends the selected address byte-for-byte, the issuer returns it byte-for-byte in the `email` claim, and every comparison is byte-for-byte. A verifier comparing byte-for-byte can never disagree with the browser, because the same bytes flow through the whole protocol — case-insensitive matching would only be needed if some party canonicalized, and none does.

issues.title: Allow issuers to assert the deliverability of the email
issues.author: samuelgoto
issues.body:
Currently, `email_verified` allows issuers to assert that the user owns the email, but not whether the email is in a deliverable state, for example, whether the user's inbox is full or not (there are probably a lot more conditions for deliverability).

Deliverability is particularly important for relying parties, which use email not just for login but also for re-engagement (e.g. newsletters, notifications, etc).

We should consider introducing a mechanism that allows email providers to make some sort of assertion about deliverability.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
lets get feedback from verifiers -- the verifier is needing to trust the signal from the provider -- there is nuance as you call out on what deliverability means -- and some of the states you list are temporal vs it being an email like identifier 

The reality could be that anyone that really wants to know deliverability will send an email ...

issues.title: Replace WebAuthn authentication with an issuer login URL (FedCM Login Status continuation)
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Problem

A token request can arrive with no valid cookie: the user is logged out of the issuer, or never logged in on this device. The spec's current answer is a WebAuthn challenge/response exchange (`webauthn_supported`, `webauthn_challenge`, `webauthn_response`, the `webauthn_state` cookie). Nothing implements it, and it hardwires one authentication method into the protocol.

## Proposal

Adopt the FedCM Login Status continuation instead. The login flow only fixes the session; the token and every error always come from the issuance endpoint, on a verified signed request.

1. The browser sends the normal signed token request. No valid cookie → the issuer returns **401** with `{"error": "authentication_required", "login_url": "https://accounts.issuer.example/login"}`.
2. The browser opens `login_url` in a browser-controlled popup, first-party context. The user authenticates however the issuer wants — password, passkey, anything. WebAuthn becomes an implementation detail of the issuer's login page, invisible to this protocol.
3. The login page signals completion via the FedCM Login Status API (`Set-Login: logged-in` header, or `navigator.login.setStatus("logged-in")`). The browser closes the popup.
4. The browser retries the token request — a new signed POST, same key pair, fresh `created`, now carrying the session cookies. The issuer processes it as an ordinary token request and returns the EVT or an error.
5. If the retry again returns `authentication_required`, the browser stops and surfaces the error to the RP. One retry, no loop.

## What this removes

`webauthn_supported` metadata, the challenge/response round trip, and the `webauthn_state` challenge-state dance. The issuer holds no protocol-visible state: the login popup and the retry are independent, ordinary exchanges. The invariant that an EVT is only ever produced in response to a verified signed token request is preserved — which is why the FedCM `continue_on` / `IdentityProvider.resolve(token)` model is NOT proposed: it delivers the token from the popup page, outside the signed exchange, and would need the original request's key context carried into the login session.

## Privacy

`login_url` is issuer-origin and carries nothing about the RP, preserving the three-party model. The email address SHOULD NOT appear in `login_url` — the retry carries it.

## Open questions

- Member on the existing `authentication_required` error, or a distinct `login_required` error code (OIDC's name for this)?
- Where the popup/`Set-Login` choreography is specified — it is browser behavior, so likely the W3C Email Verification API, with this document defining only the `login_url` member and the retry semantics.

comments.author: agektmr
comments.body: Loop through all of the keys in jwks.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Before we make kid optional, worth checking whether that’s actually the right call. I pulled JWKS from a few major OIDC issuers — Google’s own standard id_token JWKS, Firebase’s securetoken, Microsoft’s Azure AD v2, and GitLab — every single key across all of them carries a kid. The only JWKS I found without kid on any key is the one from #43 — Google’s EVT-specific signer — and per that thread, that’s a signing-infra limitation Google’s own team said they’re fixing, not a deliberate design choice.

Given that, I’d lean toward making kid required in the EVT header rather than optional-with-a-fallback-algorithm. That matches what every other JWKS in the wild already does, keeps verifiers simple (exact match, no “try every key” loop with its own edge cases), and puts the burden back on Google to finish the infra fix they already said was coming — rather than baking a permanent workaround into the spec for what looks like a temporary gap.

issues.title: Remove references (e.g. parsing) to SD-JWT
issues.author: samuelgoto
issues.body:
This issue came up as part of this discussion https://github.com/dickhardt/email-verification/issues/21#issuecomment-5398510999

We should decide whether we want to tell verifiers to parse the EVT as a full SD-JWT or not (e.g. should parsing fail if the holder decides to add things to the selective disclosure list).

If we decide not to support SD-JWTs, then we should say so, and allow verifiers to fail when the verifier doesn't parse the EVT as an SD-JWT.

If we do decide to say that the EVT is an SD-JWT than we should reuse the parsing algorithms (and existing libraries) of SD-JWT.

Either option works for me, to address this I just want the spec to be clear about whether the EVT is, in fact, a valid SD-JWT (and requires parsing it as such) or if the EVT is, in fact, a JWT and KB separated by a `~` (e.g. doesn't support having multiple `~`s).

pulls.title: Align with draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key-08
pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Signature-Key -08 is not backward compatible with -07, and this draft was written against -07. A token request serialized per -01 of this draft is rejected by an issuer implementing this branch, and vice versa. There is nothing to negotiate over, so both ends of a deployment move together.

## Breaking changes tracked from Signature-Key -08

- **`hwk` `alg` is now REQUIRED and fully specified.** It was forbidden in -07. Added to every `Signature-Key` example.
- **The polymorphic `EdDSA` identifier is forbidden**, deprecated by RFC 9864. Replaced with `Ed25519` in the browser's key, the default when `signing_alg_values_supported` is absent, the EVT header, the KB-JWT header, and every example including the base64url ones.
- **The algorithm comes from the key's `alg`**, never derived from `kty` and `crv`. A key whose `kty` or `crv` disagrees with its `alg` is rejected rather than resolved in favor of either.
- **`hwk` `kid` went from SHOULD NOT to MUST NOT.** The key is inline, so a `kid` selects nothing.
- **Verifier-side `signature-key` coverage went from SHOULD to MUST.** Coverage was already required of signers here; the issuer-side obligation was missing.
- **Signers MUST NOT send the `alg` signature parameter** and verifiers MUST ignore it, per RFC 9421 Section 3.3.7.
- **`unsupported_scheme` added**; unknown-scheme rejection is now mandatory and conformance-testable.
- **`supported_algorithms` removed from `Signature-Error`** in favor of `Accept-Signature-Alg`.

## Other changes

- `signing_alg_values_supported` must carry fully-specified identifiers, and states what it must not contain: `EdDSA`, `none`, `Prohibited` algorithms, and the symmetric MAC identifiers.
- The key's `alg` is carried into the EVT `cnf.jwk`, so the RP verifies the KB-JWT under a fully-specified algorithm rather than one derived from the key. The KB-JWT header `alg` must match it, and the RP rejects a KB-JWT where the two disagree.
- Added the `Signature-Error` response header to signature error responses, with a table mapping each failure case to its code, plus `Accept-Signature-Scheme`, `Accept-Signature-Alg`, and `required_input`.
- Added an Algorithm Determination subsection to Security Considerations giving the reason for these rules.
- Document History gained a `-02` entry recording all of the above.

Draft builds clean with `make`.

> and MUST also cover `cookie`

didn't we agree that we weren't including the `cookie` in the signature and were relying on content-digest instead?
is 60 seconds enough to account to clock skew between datacenters? is there some more established value that we can pick here from other specs rather than this arbitrary value?

It was pre-existing text carried forward by this PR's rewrite. The requirement is now gone: covering `cookie` is RECOMMENDED when the header is available to the signer at signing time, and an issuer MUST NOT reject a request solely because it is not covered. The normative change is in #17; the corrected wording lands here when the stack merges.

Agreed it was arbitrary. Changed to 300 seconds in d13bf2a. There is no single established value, but the conventions cluster at minutes: RFC 8725 puts clock-skew leeway at "no more than a few minutes", and Kerberos defaults to 5 minutes of allowable skew. Device clocks skew by minutes, not seconds, so 60 seconds would reject real users. The window is not load-bearing for security: a replayed request yields an EVT bound to the original browser's key through `cnf`, so replay gains an attacker no token another party can use. The draft now cites RFC 8725 for the choice.

pulls.title: Define "valid email address" as the WHATWG production
pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Closes #2.

The draft told issuers to verify the `email` field "contains a syntactically valid email address" without saying what that means.

RFC 5322 is the obvious citation and the wrong one. It admits comments, folding whitespace, and quoted local parts that no provider issues and no browser accepts from a user, and full implementations disagree at the edges. The WHATWG **valid e-mail address** production is a deliberate narrowing of RFC 5322 written for exactly this problem, and the browser has *already applied it* before the protocol starts — the user supplies the address through a control validated against that production. Citing it makes the issuer's check and the browser's the same check.

Adds a **Valid Email Address** section defining the term once, applying to the token request `email` field, the EVT `email` claim, and issued private addresses.

The production is willfully non-compliant with RFC 5322. The draft now says so rather than leaving a reader to discover it, and notes the consequence: an issuer whose users hold addresses outside the production cannot verify them through this protocol.

> **Stacked on #14** — base is `signature-key-08-alignment`. Merge that first.

pulls.title: Cover the request body with Content-Digest
pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Closes #3.

The email address being verified travels in the JSON request body. The covered components were `@method`, `@authority`, `@path`, `signature-key`, and `cookie` — none of which reach the body. **The signature attested to a request without attesting to which address it asked for.** A party that captured the request could substitute a different address within the 60-second `created` window and the signature would still verify.

Changes:

- The browser MUST send `Content-Digest` (RFC 9530) over the request body; `sha-256` MUST be supported and SHOULD be used.
- `content-digest` added to the required covered components.
- The issuer MUST **recompute** the digest against the bytes it received. Verifying the signature over `content-digest` establishes only that the header was signed, not that it describes the body that arrived — the recomputation is what ties the two together. Stated as an explicit step, and required before acting on the body.
- Examples updated with a real `sha-256` digest of `{"email":"user@example.com"}`.
- Request Integrity bullet in Security Considerations updated to say what the body coverage buys.

> **Stacked on #15** — base is `email-syntax-whatwg`. Merge #14 → #15 → this.

pulls.title: Make coverage of the cookie component optional
pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Closes #11.

@cbiesinger's objection is decisive: Chrome cannot produce this. The Cookie header is attached by the network stack *after* the request has been constructed and signed, so the value to be covered does not exist at signing time. As written, the MUST excluded the main browser implementation.

The property it bought — binding the authenticating cookie to the request that carries it — is real, but it is not one the protocol depends on. The user is authenticated by the cookie and the request is bound to the browser's key by the signature, whether or not the two are bound to each other. That answers @cbiesinger's "what is the value of including it" directly, in the document.

Changes:

- `cookie` MAY be covered when the Cookie header is present; an issuer MUST NOT reject a request solely because it is not covered, and MUST verify over whatever components the request does list.
- The **Cookie Binding** bullet in Security Considerations is restated as an optional property rather than a guarantee, naming what is lost when it is absent.
- Dropped `cookie` from the `Signature-Input` examples, so the canonical form is the one every implementation can produce. The requests still *send* `Cookie:` — the examples now show exactly the case this PR permits.
- The WebAuthn note updated to match; nothing in that exchange depended on the coverage.

pulls.title: Make the issuer identifier an HTTPS origin
pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Closes #7.

@samuelgoto flagged that the browser spec enforces `https://issuer.example` while the draft says `issuer.example`. Resolved in favor of the **origin**, matching the `iss` claim of OpenID Connect and the issuer of RFC 8414 — the values this one has to be comparable to. It's also what's already shipping.

**The DNS record keeps a host name.** A TXT record holding `https://` is redundant when no other scheme is permitted, and a scheme in a DNS record is not a DNS-shaped value. Instead the identifier is *derived*: `https://` + host, no port, no path, no trailing slash. New **Issuer Identifier** section states that derivation once, so it isn't re-implied at each use, and requires every comparison to be byte-for-byte on the derived string — no scheme defaulting, port normalization, or trailing-slash tolerance.

Resolution now reads:

1. DNS TXT → `issuer.example`
2. Issuer identifier → `https://issuer.example`
3. Fetch `https://issuer.example/.well-known/email-verification`
4. Metadata `issuer` MUST equal `https://issuer.example`
5. EVT `iss` MUST equal `https://issuer.example`

Step 4 is new. Added the `issuer` member to the metadata document and required a fetching party to reject a document whose `issuer` does not match the identity it was fetched under — the RFC 8414 §3.3 check. Signature-Key -08 added exactly this for its own discovery after issue #12 there; the same gap existed here, and it's what stops a document served at one identity from claiming another.

Recomputed the base64url EVT payload example.

pulls.title: Add Security Considerations for DNS delegation
pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Closes #6.

@dennisjackson raised this from Viktor's point: the delegation rests on an unauthenticated DNS TXT record and the document said nothing about it. Design Rationale defended DNS delegation on deployment grounds only.

**The two lookups are not equally valuable to an attacker,** and separating them is most of the answer. Both the browser and the RP resolve the record independently.

*Spoofing the browser's resolver alone gains little.* The browser is sent to an attacker-controlled issuer and discloses the email address. It does **not** disclose credentials — cookies are scoped to the real issuer's origin and are not sent to a different one, and a WebAuthn challenge from the attacker carries the attacker's `rpId`, so no assertion usable at the real issuer is produced. This answers the "depending on how clients authenticate" clause in the original report directly. The attacker can mint an EVT, but the RP resolves the record itself and rejects an `iss` it did not derive. The exact-comparison requirement from #18 is what makes that work.

*Spoofing the RP's resolver is the attack that matters.* The resulting token is well-formed, correctly signed, and signed by the key the RP was told to trust. Nothing later in verification catches it. Stated as the residual risk of the design rather than left implied.

Recommends DNSSEC validation by RPs — they're servers, resolving on their own infrastructure, and are far better placed for it than a browser — and zone signing by email domain operators.

On Viktor's general rule that authentication decisions should never depend on DNS: the PR neither dismisses nor concedes it. The delegation is a property of an email domain; DNS is where properties of email domains live, alongside SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, which an attacker with this same capability could already forge for the same domain. And moving it to HTTPS reintroduces the web-hosting barrier the design set out to avoid. The text still says plainly that unsigned DNS is weaker than HTTPS and that a deployment without DNSSEC is accepting the risk.

> **Stacked on #18** — base is `iss-origin`. Merge #14 → #15 → #16 → #17 → #18 → this.

pulls.title: Clarify what Email Discovery is and is not
pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Closes #4.

@lonetis is right that §2.1 and §3 read as circular. The opening sentence — "Before presenting the user with email address choices, the browser discovers which email accounts have active sessions with an issuer" — reads as resolving an issuer before any address is known, while Issuer Discovery is a DNS lookup *on* the selected address.

They aren't circular; they're different operations, and the text never said so.

- **Email Discovery populates a chooser.** That's all. It is not Issuer Discovery, it does not establish who is authoritative for a domain, and it is **optional** — a browser offering addresses from its own store, or taking one the user types, enters at Email Acquisition with no discovery step.
- **Push and Pull run against issuers the browser already has a relationship with.** That's why no email address is needed to reach them, and where the apparent circularity dissolves.
- **The substantive point, which was missing entirely:** an issuer surfacing an account through Push or Pull gains *no* authority to verify it. `_email-verification.example.com` decides that. An address an issuer volunteered is subject to the same DNS lookup as one the user typed. This is @dickhardt's "DNS is always required for the browser and the verifier to know the issuer is truly authoritative, independent of what FedCM accounts say" — now in the document.

Also added a note for the ordering difference with the W3C API that @lonetis identified, alongside the two W3C divergence notes already in the text. Both orderings arrive at the same place, so this is a description to reconcile rather than a conflict to resolve.

pulls.author: dickhardt
pulls.body:
Removes the WebAuthn Authentication section, the `webauthn_supported` metadata member and example line, the WebAuthn challenge/response exchange (including the `webauthn_state` cookie dance), the token-request bullet, and the WebAuthn reference. Nothing implements this, and it hardwired one authentication method into the protocol (raised in review of #17 and #19).

A token request without a valid session now returns the existing `authentication_required` error, which gets an explicit anchor.

The replacement is under discussion in #26: the issuer returns a login URL, the browser opens it in a first-party popup, completion is signaled via the FedCM Login Status API, and the browser retries the signed token request. The login flow only fixes the session — the token and every error always come from the issuance endpoint, so how the user authenticates (WebAuthn or anything else) is the login page's business, not the protocol's.
